installation.note: cd is a built-in shell command available in all Linux shells by default

overview.summary: cd (change directory) is used to navigate between directories in the Linux filesystem. It's one of the most fundamental commands for moving around your system. Unlike most commands, cd is built into the shell itself, not a separate program.
when_to_use: Navigate using absolute or relative paths

syntax.description: Change to the specified directory. Without arguments, cd returns to the home directory.

misconceptions.title: cd is a program like other commands
misconceptions.misconception: cd is an external program stored in /bin or /usr/bin
misconceptions.reality: cd is a built-in shell command, not a separate program. It's part of the shell itself (bash, zsh, etc.), which is why it can change the shell's current directory. External programs can't change the shell's directory.
misconceptions.tip: cd is special - it's built into your shell, which is why 'which cd' shows nothing or an alias.

misconceptions.title: cd shows the new directory path
misconceptions.misconception: cd displays the directory you changed to
misconceptions.reality: cd produces no output on success (except when using cd -). Use 'pwd' to see your current directory, or configure your prompt to show it.
misconceptions.tip: Use pwd to verify your location after cd. Or configure your shell prompt to always show the current directory.

misconceptions.title: cd creates directories
misconceptions.misconception: cd will create a directory if it doesn't exist
misconceptions.reality: cd only changes to existing directories. Use 'mkdir' first to create directories, then cd into them.
misconceptions.tip: Create directories with mkdir before using cd. Or use mkdir -p path/to/new/dir && cd path/to/new/dir

common_pitfalls.description: Directories with spaces cause cd to interpret them as separate arguments
common_pitfalls.solution: Quote directory names with spaces: cd 'My Documents' or cd "My Documents". Or escape spaces with backslash: cd My\ Documents.

common_pitfalls.description: Using relative paths when you think you're using absolute paths
common_pitfalls.solution: Absolute paths start with /. Relative paths don't. Use pwd first to know where you are, then construct paths accordingly.

common_pitfalls.description: Linux is case-sensitive, so Documents and documents are different
common_pitfalls.solution: Match the exact case of directory names. Use tab completion to avoid typos.

common_pitfalls.description: Losing track of where you are after multiple cd commands
common_pitfalls.solution: Use pwd to check your current directory. Configure your prompt to show the current path. Use cd - to go back to previous directory.

best_practices: Use tab completion to avoid typos and see available directories
Use pwd after cd if unsure of your location
Quote directory names with spaces: cd 'My Folder'
Use ~ for home directory shortcuts: cd ~/Documents
Use .. to navigate up the directory tree
Use cd - to toggle between two directories
Use absolute paths when scripting for reliability
Check directory exists with ls before using cd
performance_tips: cd is instant - it's a built-in command with no performance impact
Tab completion speeds up navigation and reduces errors
Using ~ and relative paths saves typing
cd - is faster than typing full paths when toggling directories

additional_notes.builtin: cd is a shell builtin, not a separate program. This is why it can change the shell's working directory
additional_notes.error_handling: cd without arguments always goes to home directory, even if you're already there
additional_notes.scripting: In scripts, use absolute paths or verify directory exists first. cd can cause scripts to fail if directory doesn't exist.
additional_notes.prompt_integration: Many shells configure prompts to show current directory (PS1 with \w or \W)
additional_notes.directory_stack: Advanced users can use pushd/popd for directory stack management
